summary: This document defines Multi-Protocol BGP procedures that let BGP speakers exchange Route Target reachability information. That information can build a route distribution graph that limits how far VPN routes propagate between autonomous systems or clusters. It updates RFC 4364.

eli5.summary: Instead of sending every private-network map to every router, routers say which maps they want. Then each only receives the ones it needs, saving effort.

questions: constrained route distribution bgp mpls vpn
how does rt constrain reduce vpn routes
subtitle: Letting BGP routers say which VPN Route Targets they care about, so they only receive the VPN routes they need.

tldr.problem: In BGP/MPLS VPNs, route reflectors and inter-AS routers can end up carrying every VPN route in the network, even ones none of their clients use.
tldr.mechanism: Routers advertise Route Target membership as a new kind of MP-BGP NLRI. Peers use it to send only VPN routes whose Route Targets the receiver has asked for, building a route distribution graph.
tldr.outcome: Route reflectors only handle VPN routes used by their direct clients, and operators can filter VPN scope across AS borders. The benefit grows with how sparse VPN membership is. The RFC updates RFC 4364.

today: RFC 4684 is a Proposed Standard. It updates RFC 4364 and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Route Target Scaling Problem
sections.content:
In BGP/MPLS IP VPNs, provider edge (PE) routers use Route Target (RT) extended communities to decide which routes go into which VRFs. Within an iBGP mesh, a PE router only needs routes carrying Route Targets for VRFs that have local customer attachments.

Autonomous systems often use route reflection to make it easier to bring up a new PE router and to limit the size of the iBGP mesh. When VPNs have members in more than one autonomous system, the number of routes carried by inter-cluster or inter-AS distribution routers becomes an important consideration.

RFC 4364 suggests Cooperative Route Filtering between route reflectors. This RFC is designed to supersede that for VPN-related uses. It adds support for multiple autonomous systems and asymmetric VPN topologies such as hub-and-spoke, by reusing BGP itself to carry the filtering information, including route reflection, confederations and inter-AS loop detection.
sections.eli5: Imagine a mail room that has to store every club's newsletters, even for clubs nobody in the building joined. This RFC lets the mail room learn which clubs people joined.

sections.title: The Core Idea: Membership Flows One Way, Routes the Other
sections.content:
A router advertises RT membership information, an NLRI of the form {origin-as#, route-target}. A receiver then limits its VPN route advertisements to peers that have advertised matching Route Targets. This effectively builds a route distribution graph, and VPN routes flow in the inverse direction of the membership information.

The mechanism applies to any BGP NLRI that uses Route Targets to control distribution, such as VPLS. Standard RFC 4364 inter-AS behavior can be seen as a dense-mode approach, in analogy with multicast routing protocols, while this mechanism pays off when VPN membership is sparse.
sections.eli5: Routers shout "send me this kind of map!" in one direction, and the maps travel back the other way along the same path.

sections.title: Distribution Between Autonomous Systems
sections.content:
The RFC works an example with ASes a to j in an ad hoc graph. A VPN with customer sites in AS a and AS i uses a single Route Target. Ideally the flooding graph leaves out ASes c, g, h and j: c and j are leaves that do not need the information, while g and h are not on the shortest inter-AS path between e and i, so standard BGP path selection excludes them.

Including the origin AS number in the NLRI lets speakers use ordinary rules, such as AS-path length, to prune duplicate paths while still keeping the information needed to reach every AS that advertised the Route Target. If AS j also joins the VPN, AS f advertises two RT membership NLRIs to AS e, one for origin AS i and one for origin AS j. Advertising only one would lose the information needed to prune the longer path through g and h.
sections.eli5: Each town only sends the parcel down the shortest road to the towns that asked for it, and skips the long detours and the towns that did not ask.

sections.title: Distribution Inside an Autonomous System
sections.content:
For membership information from other ASes, standard BGP route selection and advertisement already create the needed state in a transit AS. Membership that originates inside the AS needs more care, because several PE routers may source the same {origin-as#, route-target}.

When processing RT membership NLRIs from internal iBGP peers, a speaker must consider all available iBGP paths for a given RT prefix when building the outbound route filter, not only the best path. When advertising locally sourced membership to an iBGP peer, two rules apply:

  • To a route-reflector client, the Originator attribute is set to the advertiser's router-id and the Next-hop to the local address for that session. This keeps the originator from dropping a membership NLRI reflected back to it, so the reflector can tell the client to send VPN routes towards it.
  • To a non-client peer, if the best path came from a non-client and an alternative path exists from a client, the client path's attributes are advertised. This lets any speaker in the mesh signal the interest of its clients.

These procedures assume the route reflection topology would already work for IPv4 unicast, for instance with contiguous clusters. The authors note an alternative of per-PE routes of the form {originator-id, route-target} aggregated at the network edge, but rejected it because it needs more routing information inside an AS.
sections.eli5: Inside one town, the post office keeps every street's request, not just the nearest one, so it never forgets a house that wants the parcel.

sections.title: The Route Target Membership NLRI
sections.content:
Membership is carried in BGP UPDATE messages using the MP_REACH_NLRI and MP_UNREACH_NLRI attributes. The (AFI, SAFI) pair is (AFI=1, SAFI=132). The Next Hop is read as IPv4 when its length is 4 octets and as IPv6 when it is 16 octets.

The NLRI is a prefix of 0 to 96 bits: a 4-octet origin AS followed by an 8-octet route target. Except for the default route target, which is a zero-length prefix, the minimum prefix length is 32 bits. Shorter prefixes can stand for groups of route targets, such as all those assigned by one Global Administrator.

The default route target tells a peer you want all VPN routes, for example a route reflector speaking to one of its PE clients.
sections.eli5: The request card has the sender's town number and the club's code. A blank card means "send me everything."

sections.title: Capability and Operation
sections.content:
A speaker that wants to exchange membership information advertises the Multiprotocol Extensions Capability for that (AFI, SAFI) pair. It may take part without using the information to filter VPN output, though this is discouraged.

A VPN route should be sent to a peer if that peer advertised either the default membership NLRI or one containing any Route Target in the route's extended communities. On receiving an advertisement or withdrawal of membership, a speaker re-examines its RIB-OUTs for matching routes and sends the minimum set of VPN updates needed to move to the new graph.

Implementations SHOULD send an End-of-RIB marker for the membership (AFI, SAFI) as a hint that the initial exchange is complete, even if graceful restart is not enabled. A speaker that delays VPN updates until it receives the marker MUST bound the delay, and 60 seconds should be used by default.
sections.eli5: When a router has finished listing everything it wants, it says "that is all." Others wait for that, but never longer than a minute.

sections.title: Deployment and Security
sections.content:
The mechanism limits a route reflector to the VPN routes used by its direct clients, instead of the total number of VPN routes on the network. A reflector's load can then be reduced by splitting its PE routers into more clusters, a localized change. Operators can also filter inbound RT membership advertisements to control which VPN routes cross a border. For instance, a spoke RT used only inside an AS can be left out of what is advertised externally. The RFC assumes ASes agree on an RT assignment convention, and treats RT translation at the border as a local decision.

The RFC does not alter the security properties of BGP-based VPNs. Filters built from RT membership are not intended for security. Between administrative domains, incoming and outgoing NLRIs should also be filtered by other means, and implementations SHOULD provide ways to filter RT membership information.
sections.eli5: This helps big routers do less work, but it is a convenience, not a lock. For safety you still check mail at the border by other means.
